summary: Defines a number of tests that can be used to describe the performance of network interconnect devices such as routers and bridges. It was replaced by RFC 2544.

eli5.summary: Like a standard race for network boxes, so that when two companies say their box is fast, you can compare them fairly.

questions: how to measure frame loss rate
how do you test network performance
subtitle: Standard tests for measuring network device performance fairly

tldr.problem: Network vendors claim their devices are fast, but without standard tests, these claims cannot be fairly compared. Different testing methods produce incompatible results.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1944 defines a series of standardized benchmarking tests that measure throughput, latency, frame loss, and other key performance metrics using controlled test conditions and specific reporting formats.
tldr.outcome: This allows network engineers to make fair comparisons between different devices and vendors. The RFC was superseded by RFC 2544, which added further improvements to the methodology.

today: RFC 1944 is an Informational RFC and was superseded by RFC 2544 in May 1996, which provides an updated and extended benchmarking methodology. RFC 2544 added additional tests and refined the procedures based on experience gained since RFC 1944 was published.

sections.title: The Problem of Device Claims
sections.content: Network vendors often use marketing claims about their devices' performance, sometimes exaggerating or using non-standard test methods that make their products look better than competing devices. Without a uniform way to measure and report performance, buyers cannot reliably compare routers, bridges and other interconnect devices. This RFC defines a set of standardized tests and reporting methods so that vendors use the same rules when claiming performance, and customers can compare results from different vendors on equal ground.
sections.eli5: If one company says their router is really fast but does not say how they tested it, you cannot trust that it is better than another router. This RFC creates fair test rules so you can believe the numbers.

sections.title: Setting Up the Test
sections.content: The RFC describes two main ways to set up equipment for testing. The preferred method uses a single test device (called a tester) that both sends test traffic to the device being tested (called the DUT) and receives the traffic back. This lets the tester verify that all sent frames arrived correctly. Alternatively, separate transmitting and receiving equipment can be used, though this requires more careful coordination. The DUT must be configured with all supported protocols enabled, matching how it would actually be used in the real world. The exact configuration used in the tests must be documented in the results.
sections.eli5: You need a machine that throws packets at the router and catches what comes back, so you can count if anything got lost or broken on the way.

sections.title: The Main Performance Tests
sections.content: RFC 1944 defines six core benchmarking tests. Throughput measures the maximum rate at which a device can forward frames without losing any. Latency measures how long it takes for a frame to travel through the device. Frame loss rate tests how many packets are discarded at increasing data rates. Back-to-back frames tests how many consecutive frames with no gaps between them the device can handle. System recovery measures how quickly the device returns to normal operation after being overloaded. Reset tests how long it takes to recover from a hardware or software reset. Each test is performed at multiple frame sizes (from 64 bytes to 1518 bytes on Ethernet) to characterize performance across different packet sizes.
sections.eli5: You measure how fast it forwards packets, how long packets take to get through, how many it loses under stress, how many it can handle in a burst, how it recovers when overloaded, and how long it takes to restart.

sections.title: Testing Under Realistic Conditions
sections.content: The core tests should be repeated under various real-world conditions. These modifiers include adding broadcast frames (1% of traffic) to test if special broadcast handling slows down normal forwarding. Management frames (SNMP queries) are added to simulate network management activity. Routing updates test whether processing routing protocol messages affects forwarding performance. Filters test both a single filter condition and a more complex set of 25 filter rules to see how access control lists impact performance. The document also covers testing with multiple source and destination addresses, bidirectional traffic, and traffic from multiple input ports simultaneously to better match real network scenarios.
sections.eli5: Besides simple packet tests, you also measure how the router handles management commands, incoming updates that change the routing table, and rules that decide which packets to forward.

sections.title: How to Report Results
sections.content: The RFC specifies reporting formats for each test. Throughput results are reported as a graph with frame size on the x-axis and frame rate on the y-axis, typically including both the theoretical maximum for the media and the measured performance. Latency is reported in a table with columns for frame size, the data rate tested, the media type, and measured latency values. Frame loss rate is also plotted as a graph. All other results (back-to-back, recovery, reset) are reported in table format. Vendors are required to include the protocol tested, the exact DUT configuration, the software version, all frame sizes tested, and the values of any test parameters. This level of detail ensures that buyers can understand exactly what was tested and can trust the reported numbers.
sections.eli5: Results are shown as graphs or tables so you can see not just one number but how performance changes as packets get bigger or there are more rules to apply.

sections.title: Testing Multiple Devices Together
sections.content: While the primary focus is testing a single device, RFC 1944 also covers how to benchmark chains of multiple devices. For example, a LAN-to-WAN-to-LAN configuration might route Ethernet traffic through one device, across a WAN link, and through another device to Ethernet again. This methodology allows vendors to report end-to-end performance of complex systems. However, such testing yields aggregate benchmarks that may not show asymmetries in behavior between the individual devices or latencies introduced by other equipment. The testing process must account for all the complexities of the actual system being benchmarked.
sections.eli5: If you want to test how fast packets go through multiple routers chained together, you can measure the whole chain, but you have to be careful because the slowdown might come from any part of it.

items.label: Latency

items.label: Frame Loss Rate

items.desc: Maximum number of consecutive frames handled without loss.

items.desc: Time to return to normal after an overload condition.
